To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

“The core clock genes Per 2, Bmal 1, Clock and C ry1 do not oscillation in canine peripheral blood mono nuclear cells in vivo, but do so in cultured cells, and that this response is dependent upon exposure to serum”.
the clock genes Bmal1, Per2 and Cry1 oscillate with a 24 h rhythm in the peripheral blood mononucleated cells of healthy dogs.

(i) all core clock gene transcripts examined were rhythmically expressed in the PBMCs of healthy dogs; (ii) the expression profiles of these genes were similar to those of other peripheral tissues; (iii) the serum from horses was capable of synchronizing the circadian expression of clock genes in PBMCs from dogs; and (iv) the serum from dogs was not able to synchronize the circadian expression in equine PBMCs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the circadian regulation of physiological processes in the horse.
the circadian control of physiological and behavioural processes and the identification of novel biomarkers of circadian dysfunction in the horse.
the identification of the molecular basis of circadian timing in the horse and the application of these findings to improve our understanding and management of disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the circadian system of dogs and horses is not yet understood and that further research in this area is needed.
the core clock gene expression in canine PBMCs is not under direct SCN control, but can be influenced by the circadian clock in other tissues via the release of humoral signals.
, as yet, there is no evidence for a circadian clock in PBMCs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the horse circadian clock is functional in vivo, and in vitro, but that the horse PBMC clock is functional only in vitro.
in horses and dogs, the circadian clock genes are expressed in peripheral blood cells in vivo, but that the clockwork is turned off in PBMCs.
the horse circadian system, at least in the periphery, is a robust one.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the circadian clock in PBMCs is not functional in vivo, but can be induced by serum factors from another species.

it is not possible to study the molecular clockwork of peripheral tissues in vivo in horses or dogs using PBMCs, and that the use of serum as a source of clock-resetting factors may provide a useful tool for the study of circadian timing in vitro.
the core clock gene expression in PBMCs is not driven by the master clock in vivo, but is responsive to serum signals in vitro.
